topics.title: Chapter 34 — File Descriptors
topics.summary: A file descriptor is a small nonnegative integer that indexes a process’s descriptor table. It can refer to a regular file, pipe, socket, or other supported object. The descriptor number is meaningful only while that table entry remains open; after closure, the same number can be reused for an unrelated object. The central programming rule is simple: interpret the documented return value of every operation. A request for a certain byte count is not a guarantee that exactly that many bytes moved. Error handling, partial progress, and cleanup are part of the operation’s semantics, not optional additions. [ R11 , R12 , R13 , R47 ]

topics.title: 34.1 Descriptor tables
topics.summary: A descriptor-table entry refers to an open file description or another kernel-managed open object. Descriptor flags such as close-on-exec belong to the descriptor, while file status flags and the current offset have their own sharing rules. Treat ownership explicitly. A function that borrows a descriptor must not close it unless the contract transfers ownership. A function that returns a newly opened descriptor must document who closes it. Copying the integer does not create a new kernel reference; dup does.

topics.title: 34.2 Standard input
topics.summary: Descriptor 0 conventionally represents standard input, accessed through STDIN_FILENO . It may be a terminal, file, pipe, or another redirected source. A program should not assume keyboard input merely because it reads descriptor 0. Reading standard input until end of file makes a utility composable. The same implementation can then process an interactive stream, a redirected file, or a pipeline without knowing which source supplied the bytes.

topics.title: 34.3 Standard output
topics.summary: Descriptor 1 conventionally represents standard output. Machine-readable results should normally go there, while diagnostics go elsewhere. Mixing progress messages into a binary or structured output stream can corrupt downstream processing. A write to standard output can fail or complete partially. Redirection to a full filesystem, a broken pipe, or another failing endpoint changes the result even when the program’s internal calculation succeeded. Output completion is part of overall success.

topics.title: 34.4 Standard error
topics.summary: Descriptor 2 conventionally represents standard error. It gives diagnostics a separate destination from normal output, allowing users to redirect or capture them independently. Separation is a convention supported by descriptor setup, not a guarantee of distinct physical devices. A shell can redirect both descriptors to one file. Diagnostic code should also avoid overwriting the original error information before reporting it.

topics.title: 34.5 open
topics.summary: open resolves a pathname and requests access with specified flags. It returns a descriptor on success and -1 on failure. Creation flags require a permission mode, which is affected by the process’s file-creation mask and other applicable policy. [ R47 ] Choose destructive behavior deliberately. O_TRUNC can discard existing contents; O_EXCL with creation can require that a new name be created. O_CLOEXEC establishes close-on-exec atomically with opening on the reference platform, avoiding a separate setup window in multithreaded code.

topics.title: 34.6 read
topics.summary: read(fd, buffer, count) returns a nonnegative byte count or -1 on error. A positive result smaller than count is a successful short read. For a positive requested count, zero indicates end of file for the stream-oriented uses considered here. [ R11 ] On EINTR , retry when the operation’s contract and cancellation policy call for it. On a nonblocking descriptor, EAGAIN or EWOULDBLOCK means that readiness must be awaited; a tight retry loop merely wastes CPU. Never process bytes beyond the returned count.

topics.title: 34.8 close
topics.summary: close releases a descriptor reference and can report errors associated with outstanding I/O. On Linux, do not blindly retry close after an error: the descriptor number may already have been released and reused. A retry could close an unrelated resource. [ R13 ] This is a documented portability boundary. POSIX.1-2024 specifies different EINTR behavior from Linux’s established behavior. The examples in this book use the Linux rule explicitly rather than presenting one retry pattern as universal. Closing also does not by itself establish durable storage.

LECTURE NARRATION
A file descriptor is a small nonnegative integer that indexes a process’s descriptor table. It can refer to a regular file, pipe, socket, or other supported object.
